hero.title: The Emotion Wheel
hero.lead:
An emotion wheel is a map of feelings: broad families at the center — happy, sad, angry, afraid, surprised, disgusted — with precise words fanning outward. Most of us run on about four feelings ("fine," "tired," "stressed," "bad"); most of what we experience sits in the gaps.

Closing the gaps pays: "bad" gives you nothing to do; "disappointed," "resentful" and "overwhelmed" each point somewhere different. Below: the core families, a table of precise words, why naming helps, and how to pair the wheel with a daily mood log.

sections.heading: Where the wheel comes from, and what it's for
sections.html:
The best-known wheels descend from Robert Plutchik's 1980 wheel — eight primary emotions in opposing pairs, intensity running rim to center (annoyance, anger, rage) — and Gloria Willcox's 1982 Feeling Wheel, built for therapy rooms: core feelings inside, rings of specific words out, so a client stuck on "I feel bad" has somewhere to move.

Which version barely matters; the move is the point: start with the broad family and step outward one ring at a time until a word settles. There's no correct answer; the wheel diagnoses nothing.

sections.heading: The core emotion families
sections.html:
Six families cover most experience; calm and strong aren't in every wheel but stop good days going unrecorded.

  • Happy — something you value is present or going well.
  • Sad — something you value is missing or lost.
  • Angry — something you value was crossed or blocked.
  • Afraid — a threat to something you value, focused forward.
  • Surprised — the world didn't match expectation.
  • Disgusted — something violates what you find acceptable.
  • Calm — nothing urgent demands your attention.
  • Strong — capacity to meet what's in front of you.

Each family reports on something different — anger marks a boundary; fear, what you're protecting; sadness, what mattered. Messages, not verdicts.

sections.heading: From core feeling to precise word
sections.html:
Find the closest row, then scan across: middle column milder, right stronger.

Core feelingMilder shadesStronger shadesOften signals
Happycontent, pleased, comfortable, amused, hopeful, curious, satisfiedjoyful, elated, delighted, thrilled, grateful, moved, exhilaratedSomething you value is present; note what
Sadwistful, low, disappointed, discouraged, tired, flat, nostalgicgrieving, heartbroken, despairing, hopeless, empty, anguishedA loss, an absence, an unmet expectation
Angryannoyed, irritated, impatient, frustrated, put out, indignantfurious, enraged, betrayed, seething, contemptuous, bitterA boundary crossed or blocked — name it
Afraiduneasy, nervous, apprehensive, cautious, self-conscious, tenseanxious, panicked, terrified, dread, overwhelmed, helplessA future threat, real or imagined — see tracking anxiety
Surprisedcurious, startled, puzzled, intrigued, unsettledshocked, stunned, astonished, dumbfounded, disorientedReality and expectation came apart
Disgusteduncomfortable, reluctant, put off, dismissive, waryrepulsed, appalled, revolted, ashamed, self-loathingA value violated — whose, and do you agree?
Calmsettled, steady, relaxed, at ease, unbothered, restedpeaceful, serene, grounded, safe, free, wholeNothing urgent — worth recording, not just passing through
Strongcapable, focused, determined, willing, engaged, preparedconfident, powerful, proud, energized, courageous, unstoppableCapacity meets demand — note what made it possible

Two words carry everything. "Stressed" is usually fear plus workload — which is louder, the deadline or the dread? "Fine" is often calm, and often exhaustion in a polite coat.

sections.heading: Why naming a feeling precisely helps
sections.html:
It turns intensity down. Affect labeling research consistently ties naming a feeling to a drop in its intensity; fifteen seconds of writing in a hard hour beats fifteen minutes of thinking.

It tells you what to do. Lonely suggests contacting someone; resentful, an unmade request; overwhelmed, subtraction, not effort. "Bad" suggests nothing — hence the scrolling.

It makes the record worth reading. "Stressed" on every difficult day flattens into a smear; anxious Mondays separated from resentful Thursdays are two problems with two solutions — a chart that tells you something.

Precision isn't analysis: name it, note it, move on — the pattern is for later.

sections.heading: Using the wheel with a 5-point scale
sections.html:
The number is comparable across time; the word makes a point interpretable later — two entries rated 2 can mean "anxious and wired" or "flat and heavy." You want both:

  1. Rate first, quickly. The scale only needs to agree with itself.
  2. Find the family. Which of the eight is closest?
  3. Step out one ring. Two fit? Log both — mixed feelings are the normal case.
  4. Add the trigger. "Resentful — unanswered email" is plenty.
  5. Stop. Thirty seconds; the habit survives on brevity.

If the word won't come, start from the body — tight, heavy, restless, hollow. A grounding exercise helps at full volume; journal prompts beat a blank field.

sections.heading: Printed wheel vs app: an honest comparison
sections.html:
A printed wheel works; always visible, it lands your eye on words you weren't looking for. But it can't remember: March's word is gone unless written down. The app's half:

  • Rating and words together in five seconds — scale, factor tag, note.
  • Charts by level and, via your notes, by kind — anxious days apart from flat ones.
  • Reminders and widgets for ordinary days, not just memorable ones.
  • iCloud sync, no account, no email — private material stays that way.
  • Export to PDF, XLSX, CSV or JSON when a therapist should see specifics.
  • AI insights over your history, free with optional premium — a mirror, not advice.

Use both: the wheel finds the word, the log keeps it. Neither is therapy or diagnosis — they're tools for noticing, where useful conversations start.

items.question: What are the core emotions on an emotion wheel?
items.answer: Most wheels use six: **happy, sad, angry, afraid, surprised and disgusted**. Many add **calm** and **strong**, which is worth having — a vocabulary that only describes difficulty leaves your good days undescribed. Everything else on the wheel is a more precise shade of one of those families.

items.question: What if I feel two things at once?
items.answer: That's the normal case, not a problem with the wheel. Relief and guilt, excitement and dread, love and resentment routinely arrive together. Log both — a mixed entry is more accurate than a clean one you had to force, and mixed feelings are usually the interesting ones.

items.question: Does naming an emotion really change anything?
items.answer: Research on *affect labeling* consistently finds that putting a feeling into words is associated with a reduction in its intensity. It also gives you somewhere to go: "lonely" suggests contacting someone, "overwhelmed" suggests removing something. "Bad" suggests nothing, which is why it's the least useful word in the log.

items.question: I can't tell what I'm feeling at all. Where do I start?
items.answer: Start with the body rather than the emotion: tight, heavy, restless, hollow, buzzing, tired. Then ask which family it's closest to and step out one ring. "Numb" and "nothing much" are real answers worth logging as themselves. Difficulty naming feelings is common and it improves with practice.

items.question: Do I still need a number if I'm writing the word down?
items.answer: Yes — they do different jobs. The number is comparable over time, which is what makes a [mood chart](/mood-journal/mood-chart/) possible; the word is what makes any single point interpretable weeks later. Two entries rated 2 can mean completely different days.

data.disclaimerText: This article is for general information only and is not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. An emotion wheel is a vocabulary tool and a mood journal is a self-tracking tool — neither diagnoses anything, and neither replaces therapy or professional care. If low mood persists most of the day for more than two weeks, if you find it consistently hard to identify or manage what you feel, or if emotions are disrupting your daily life, please talk to a doctor or therapist. If you are having thoughts of harming yourself, contact your local emergency services or a crisis helpline in your country right away — support is available now.
